specStatements.text: Each colour within the visible light spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction is called specular reflection. Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering: this is called diffuse reflection.
Colour filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths (and colour) and transmitting other wavelengths (and colour).

The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths of light are more strongly reflected. Wavelengths that are not reflected are absorbed. If all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white. If all wavelengths are absorbed the objects appears black.
Objects that transmit light are either transparent or translucent.
Students should be able to explain:
• how the colour of an object is related to the differential absorption, transmission and reflection of different wavelengths of light by the object
• the effect of viewing objects through filters or the effect on light of passing through filters
• why an opaque object has a particular colour.

concepts.definition: The range of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect, running from red at the long-wavelength end to violet at the short-wavelength end. The colours run continuously into one another rather than being separated by gaps.

concepts.term: Narrow band of wavelength and frequency
concepts.definition: Each colour in the visible spectrum occupies a small range of wavelengths and a matching small range of frequencies, not a single value. Red occupies the longest-wavelength, lowest-frequency band; violet the shortest-wavelength, highest-frequency band.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction. Parallel rays arriving at the surface stay parallel after reflection, so a clear image is formed, as in a plane mirror.

Reflection from a rough surface, which causes scattering. Each individual ray still obeys the law of reflection, but the surface normals point in many directions, so the reflected rays leave in many directions and no image is formed.
The spreading of reflected light into many directions, caused here by the unevenness of a rough surface. Scattering is why a sheet of paper looks equally bright from almost any viewing angle.

A material that absorbs certain wavelengths (and colours) of the light falling on it and transmits the other wavelengths (and colours). A filter removes light; it never adds light of a colour that was not already present.
The passing of light through a material, rather than the light being reflected from it or absorbed by it. Transmitted light emerges on the far side of the material.
The taking in of light energy by a material, so that the light does not leave the material as light. Wavelengths that are absorbed by an object are not available to be reflected or transmitted.
The fact that a single object treats different wavelengths differently, reflecting some strongly while absorbing others. This unequal treatment of the wavelengths is what gives an object its colour.
An object that transmits no light. Light falling on it is either reflected or absorbed, and its colour is set by the wavelengths it reflects most strongly.
A surface appears white when all wavelengths are reflected equally, and black when all wavelengths are absorbed. Black is therefore the absence of reflected light rather than a reflected colour.
Describes an object that transmits light without scattering it, so a clear image can be seen through it. Window glass and clear plastic are transparent.
Describes an object that transmits light but scatters it on the way through, so light gets through but no clear image can be seen. Frosted glass, tracing paper and thin fabric are translucent.

concepts.term: Colour of an object under coloured light
concepts.definition: An object can only reflect wavelengths that are present in the light falling on it. If the illuminating light contains none of the wavelengths the object reflects, the object appears black.

misconceptions.question: Is a colour such as red a single wavelength of light?
misconceptions.correct: Each colour within the visible light spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency, so red covers a small range of wavelengths rather than one value.
misconceptions.misconception: Red is one exact wavelength, green is another exact wavelength, and so on — one number for each colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Spectrum diagrams print a single figure beside each colour, and exam questions often say 'red light of wavelength 700 nm', which makes a colour look like one fixed number.
misconceptions.correction: Take the specification wording literally: each colour has a narrow band of wavelength and a narrow band of frequency. The bands sit side by side and run into one another, which is why the visible spectrum has no gaps in it.

misconceptions.question: Do all the colours of visible light have the same frequency?
misconceptions.correct: Each colour has its own band of frequency as well as its own band of wavelength; red light has the lowest frequencies and violet the highest.
misconceptions.misconception: All visible light travels at the same speed, so all colours must share the same frequency and only the wavelength changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum and over-extend 'the same' from speed to frequency.
misconceptions.correction: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. If the speed is fixed and the wavelength changes from colour to colour, then the frequency must change too — in the opposite direction.

misconceptions.question: Which surface gives specular reflection: a smooth one or a rough one?
misconceptions.correct: Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction is specular reflection; reflection from a rough surface causes scattering and is diffuse reflection.
misconceptions.misconception: The two terms are swapped, so 'diffuse' is taken to describe the mirror-like case and 'specular' the scattered case.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words are unfamiliar and neither sounds obviously like 'mirror' or 'scattered', so students memorise the pair without a hook and then attach them the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Link 'specular' to 'spectacles' and 'speculum', both to do with mirrors: specular means mirror-like, from a smooth surface. Diffuse shares its root with 'diffused', meaning spread out — the scattering case.

misconceptions.question: Does light obey the law of reflection when it reflects from a rough surface?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Every individual ray obeys the law of reflection; the surface is uneven, so the normals point in different directions and the reflected rays leave in many directions.
misconceptions.misconception: Diffuse reflection is the case where light stops obeying the law of reflection and bounces off at random angles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The scattered ray diagram looks disordered, and students assume that disorder in the picture means the rule has broken down.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the normal at each separate point on a bumpy surface. Each normal points a different way, but at every point the angle of incidence still equals the angle of reflection. The rule holds; only the surface has changed.

misconceptions.question: Does a red filter add red to the light passing through it?
misconceptions.correct: No. A filter absorbs certain wavelengths and transmits others, so it can only remove light. A red filter transmits red because red was already present in the light.
misconceptions.misconception: The filter dyes or colours the light, so any light shone through it comes out with the filter's colour added to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The filter is visibly coloured and the emerging light matches it, so 'the filter coloured the light' looks like the obvious explanation.
misconceptions.correction: Shine pure blue light through a red filter and almost nothing comes out. If the filter were adding red, red would appear. Instead the blue is absorbed and there is no red for the filter to transmit.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the wavelengths a colour filter does not let through?
misconceptions.correct: They are absorbed by the filter.
misconceptions.misconception: The unwanted wavelengths are reflected back off the filter, in the way a coloured surface reflects its own colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the rule for opaque coloured objects, where the colours you do not see are the ones sent back, to a transparent filter without adjusting it.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others. Hold a green filter up to a bright lamp: the room behind the lamp does not gain a red glow, because the red is taken in, not sent back.

misconceptions.question: A book looks red in white light. Which wavelengths is it reflecting?
misconceptions.correct: It reflects red wavelengths most strongly, and absorbs the wavelengths that are not reflected.
misconceptions.misconception: An object shows the colour it absorbs, so a red book must be the one absorbing the red light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that colour involves both absorption and reflection but not which of the two reaches the eye, and 'the object takes in red, so it is red' sounds reasonable.
misconceptions.correction: Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour you see is the light coming off the object, so it must be made of the reflected wavelengths. The absorbed ones never reach you at all.

misconceptions.question: What is a white surface doing to the light that falls on it?
misconceptions.correct: It reflects all wavelengths equally, whereas a black surface absorbs all wavelengths.
misconceptions.misconception: White and black are the wrong way round: white surfaces take in all of the light and black surfaces send it all back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate white with emptiness and black with 'full', or they recall that black objects get hot and reason that being hot means the energy is coming back out.
misconceptions.correction: A black car roof gets far hotter in sunlight than a white one, because the black surface absorbs the energy instead of reflecting it. Reflecting every wavelength equally is what makes a surface look white.

misconceptions.question: Why does a black surface look black?
misconceptions.correct: All the wavelengths falling on it are absorbed, so almost no light is reflected back to the eye.
misconceptions.misconception: The light passes straight through the black object instead of being absorbed by it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that no light is coming back and jump to 'the light went somewhere else' — through the object — rather than accepting that the energy was taken in.
misconceptions.correction: Black objects here are opaque, so no light gets through. Hold a black card in front of a lamp and nothing shows through on the far side. The energy is absorbed and warms the card.

misconceptions.question: Is frosted glass transparent or translucent?
misconceptions.correct: It is translucent: it transmits light but scatters it, so no clear image can be seen through it.
misconceptions.misconception: 'Transparent' and 'translucent' mean the same thing — anything that lets light through is transparent.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words look and sound alike and both describe materials you can see light coming through, so students treat them as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: The test is the image, not the light. Transparent means you see a clear image through the material; translucent means light gets through but the image does not. Both transmit light, which is why the specification pairs them.

misconceptions.question: Does a rough surface such as paper reflect the light that falls on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A rough surface reflects light, but the reflection is diffuse: the light is scattered in many directions.
misconceptions.misconception: Rough or dull surfaces absorb light rather than reflecting it, and only shiny surfaces reflect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate 'reflective' with 'shiny', so a matt surface reads as one that does not reflect at all.
misconceptions.correction: You can see a sheet of white paper from every side of the room, which is only possible because it is reflecting light towards you from every angle. If it absorbed the light it would look black.

misconceptions.question: How does a red object look when it is viewed through a green filter?
misconceptions.correct: It appears black, because the green filter absorbs the red light the object reflects, and the object reflects no green.
misconceptions.misconception: The object takes on the colour of the filter, so it looks green.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything seen through a coloured filter has a colour cast, so students generalise to 'the filter makes everything its own colour'.
misconceptions.correction: The filter can only transmit wavelengths that reach it. A red object sends only red towards the green filter, and the green filter absorbs red, so no light gets through and the object looks black.

misconceptions.question: What happens when light passes through a red filter and then a blue filter?
misconceptions.correct: Almost no light gets through: the red filter absorbs the blue, and the blue filter absorbs the red that is left.
misconceptions.misconception: The two filters combine, so the light comes out as a mixture such as purple, or the second filter undoes the first and white light returns.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over the rules for mixing coloured paints or adding coloured light beams, where combining two colours makes a new colour.
misconceptions.correction: Filters act one after the other, and each one only ever subtracts. Track the light through in order: white light in, red only after the first filter, then nothing after a filter that absorbs red.

misconceptions.question: Where does the coloured light coming from a red jumper come from?
misconceptions.correct: It comes from the light source. The jumper reflects the red wavelengths of the light falling on it and absorbs the rest.
misconceptions.misconception: The object produces or gives out light of its own colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Objects appear to 'have' their colour permanently, so students treat the colour as something the object emits rather than something it does to the incoming light.
misconceptions.correction: Take the light away and the colour disappears — a red jumper is invisible in a dark room. Colour depends on the light falling on the object, which is why objects change appearance under coloured lighting.

misconceptions.question: Is the colour of an opaque object set by the light it lets through?
misconceptions.correct: No. An opaque object transmits no light; its colour is set by which wavelengths it reflects most strongly.
misconceptions.misconception: Objects are coloured because certain wavelengths pass through them, as happens with a filter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filters and coloured objects are taught close together, so the transmission explanation gets applied to solid objects as well.
misconceptions.correction: Sort the situation first. If light gets through, the object is transparent or translucent and transmission matters. If the object is opaque, only reflection and absorption are available.

misconceptions.question: Can a coloured material still transmit light?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Coloured glass and coloured plastic transmit some wavelengths and absorb others, so they do still transmit light.
misconceptions.misconception: Only clear, colourless materials transmit light; anything with a colour must be opaque.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'See-through' is learned as meaning colourless, so a coloured sheet gets filed with solid objects rather than with transmitting ones.
misconceptions.correction: A red filter is coloured and you can still see a lamp through it. Being coloured tells you which wavelengths are absorbed, not whether any light gets through at all.

misconceptions.question: A material lets light through but you cannot see a clear image. Is it opaque?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is translucent. Opaque means that no light is transmitted at all.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything you cannot see a clear image through counts as opaque.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students use 'can I see through it?' as the single test and treat a blurred view as no view, which lumps translucent materials in with opaque ones.
misconceptions.correction: Use two tests, not one. First, does any light get through? If not, it is opaque. If light does get through, ask whether the image is clear: clear means transparent, blurred means translucent.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the colours of the visible light spectrum?

options.text: Each colour has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: every colour occupies a small range of wavelengths together with a matching small range of frequencies.

options.text: Each colour has one exact wavelength and one exact frequency
options.rationale: Spectrum diagrams quote a single figure per colour, so students read a colour as one value rather than a band.

options.text: Each colour has its own wavelength but all share one frequency
options.rationale: Students who know all light travels at the same speed wrongly extend 'the same' from speed to frequency.

options.text: All the colours share a wavelength band but differ in speed
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think colour must come from a difference in wave speed; all visible light travels at the same speed in a vacuum.

mcqs.stem: Red light and violet light both lie within the visible spectrum. Which statement about their bands is correct?

options.text: The red band lies at one fixed wavelength and the violet at another
options.rationale: Treats each colour as a single wavelength value instead of the narrow band the specification describes.

options.text: The red band has longer wavelengths, so it has lower frequencies
options.rationale: Each colour holds its own band of wavelength and of frequency; red sits at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the visible spectrum.

options.text: The red band has longer wavelengths but the same frequency
options.rationale: Believing all colours share one speed and frequency (m02), only wavelength differs; but red's frequency is actually lower.

options.text: The red and violet bands cover the same range of wavelength
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the colour bands overlap completely; each colour has its own narrow band.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection?

options.text: Specular reflection is from a rough surface, and diffuse from a smooth one
options.rationale: The two terms have been swapped; neither word sounds obviously like 'mirror', so the pair is easily learned the wrong way round.

options.text: Specular reflection always obeys the law of reflection and diffuse does not
options.rationale: Every ray obeys the law of reflection in both cases; in diffuse reflection the surface normals point in different directions.

options.text: Specular reflection is from a smooth surface, diffuse from a rough one
options.rationale: The specification defines specular reflection as reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction, and diffuse reflection as reflection from a rough surface, which scatters the light.

options.text: Specular reflection sends light back and diffuse takes most of it in
options.rationale: Assumes a dull surface absorbs rather than reflects; a rough surface does reflect, but the light is scattered.

mcqs.stem: A mirror shows a clear image of a lamp, but a sheet of white paper beside it looks equally bright from every direction. Why does the paper behave differently?

options.text: Its rough surface obeys no law, so the rays leave at random angles
options.rationale: The scattered ray diagram looks disordered, so students conclude the law of reflection has broken down; in fact each ray still obeys it.

options.text: Its rough surface takes in the light and gives it out slowly
options.rationale: Equates a matt surface with an absorbing one; the paper looks bright precisely because it is reflecting light towards you.

options.text: Its rough surface transmits light while the mirror reflects it
options.rationale: Paper is opaque, so no light is transmitted through it; the difference between the two surfaces is smooth against rough.

options.text: Its rough surface scatters light into many directions
options.rationale: Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering — diffuse reflection — so light leaves towards every viewing position and no image is formed.

mcqs.stem: How does a colour filter work?

options.text: It reflects the unwanted wavelengths and lets the rest through
options.rationale: Transfers the rule for opaque coloured objects to a filter; the wavelengths that do not get through are absorbed, not sent back.

options.text: It absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits the others
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and colours, and transmitting the other wavelengths and colours.

options.text: It adds its own colour to the white light that passes through
options.rationale: The filter is coloured and the emerging light matches it, so students assume the filter dyes the light rather than removing wavelengths.

options.text: It changes the wavelength of the light passing through it
options.rationale: A filter cannot convert one wavelength into another; it only selects which of the wavelengths already present get through.

mcqs.stem: White light is shone through a blue filter. What emerges from the filter, and why?

options.text: All the colours, but with the blue much brighter than the rest
options.rationale: A filter does not brighten one colour; the other wavelengths are removed altogether rather than merely dimmed.

options.text: White light that has been dyed blue as it travelled through
options.rationale: Treats the filter as adding colour; a filter can only remove wavelengths from the light reaching it.

options.text: Blue light, because the other wavelengths are absorbed by it
options.rationale: White light contains every wavelength; the blue filter absorbs all of them except the blue band, which it transmits.

options.text: Blue light, because the other colours reflect back off it
options.rationale: Right outcome for the wrong reason — the light is blue, but the removed wavelengths are absorbed rather than reflected.

mcqs.stem: What determines the colour of an opaque object viewed in white light?

options.text: The wavelengths that the object absorbs most strongly of all
options.rationale: Absorbed light never reaches the eye, so it cannot be the light you see; students recall that absorption is involved but pick the wrong half.

options.text: The wavelengths that the object gives out when it is warm
options.rationale: Treats colour as light emitted by the object; the light seen comes from the source and is reflected by the object.

options.text: The wavelengths that the object lets through itself
options.rationale: Applies the filter explanation to a solid object; an opaque object transmits no light at all.

options.text: The wavelengths that the object reflects most strongly
options.rationale: The specification states that the colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the rest are absorbed.

mcqs.stem: A jumper appears white when it is lit by white light. What is happening to the light that falls on it?

options.text: All wavelengths are reflected equally
options.rationale: The specification states that if all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white.

options.text: All wavelengths are absorbed equally by it
options.rationale: Reverses white and black; absorbing everything would leave no reflected light and the jumper would look black.

options.text: All wavelengths pass straight through the wool
options.rationale: The jumper is opaque, so nothing is transmitted; white comes from equal reflection of every wavelength.

options.text: Only the wavelengths of white are reflected
options.rationale: There is no separate 'white wavelength' — white is the result of reflecting the whole range of visible wavelengths equally.

mcqs.stem: A piece of card looks black in a brightly lit room. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The light passes straight through the card without stopping
options.rationale: Students accept that no light comes back and assume it went through instead; the card is opaque, so nothing is transmitted.

options.text: The card reflects every wavelength that falls upon it equally
options.rationale: Reflecting all wavelengths equally is what makes a surface look white, not black.

options.text: The card absorbs all of the wavelengths of light that fall on it
options.rationale: The specification states that if all wavelengths are absorbed the object appears black, because almost no light is reflected to the eye.

options.text: The card gives out no light of its own in the lit room
options.rationale: Treats colour as emitted light; no everyday object emits its colour, yet a white card in the same room looks white.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of objects that transmit light?

options.text: They must be colourless as well as see-through
options.rationale: Coloured glass transmits light too; its colour tells you which wavelengths are absorbed, not that light is blocked.

options.text: They transmit light only when very smooth
options.rationale: Confuses transmission with specular reflection; frosted glass is rough yet still transmits light.

options.text: They are either translucent or opaque
options.rationale: An opaque object transmits no light at all, so it cannot belong in a list of objects that transmit light.

options.text: They are either transparent or translucent
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: objects that transmit light are either transparent or translucent.

mcqs.stem: Frosted bathroom glass lets light into the room, but no clear image can be seen through it. How is the glass best described?

options.text: Translucent, since it scatters the light passing through
options.rationale: Light is transmitted, so the glass is not opaque, but the scattering destroys the image — which is exactly what translucent means.

options.text: Transparent, since the light gets through the glass easily
options.rationale: Uses 'lets light through' as the whole test for transparent; a transparent material also gives a clear image.

options.text: Opaque, since there is no clear image to be seen through it
options.rationale: Treats a blurred view as no view; opaque means no light gets through at all, but this glass lights the room.

options.text: Specular, since the rough surface reflects light
options.rationale: Specular reflection describes a smooth reflecting surface and says nothing about transmitted light.

mcqs.stem: A book cover appears red in white light. Which explanation of its colour is correct?

options.text: Red is absorbed by the cover and other wavelengths reflected
options.rationale: Only reflected light reaches the eye, so absorbed wavelengths cannot be the colour that is seen.

options.text: Red is reflected and the other wavelengths absorbed
options.rationale: Differential treatment of the wavelengths gives the colour: the red band is reflected most strongly and the wavelengths not reflected are absorbed.

options.text: Red is transmitted through the cover and the rest reflected
options.rationale: Uses the filter explanation for an opaque object, which transmits no light.

options.text: Red light is given out by the cover in any conditions
options.rationale: Treats the object as a light source; in a dark room the cover shows no colour at all.

mcqs.stem: In white light a leaf looks green and a daisy petal looks white. Which explanation accounts for both?

options.text: The leaf absorbs green strongly and reflects the other wavelengths; the petal absorbs the whole range
options.rationale: Reverses reflection and absorption for the leaf, and would make the petal look black rather than white.

options.text: The leaf reflects green and absorbs the others; the petal absorbs every wavelength equally
options.rationale: The leaf is explained correctly, but absorbing all wavelengths equally produces black, not white.

options.text: The leaf transmits green light through itself, and the petal transmits the whole range of light
options.rationale: Both are opaque, so their colour comes from reflection and absorption rather than from transmission.

options.text: The leaf reflects green strongly and absorbs the other wavelengths; the petal reflects them all equally
options.rationale: Colour comes from differential reflection and absorption: unequal reflection gives green, and equal reflection of every wavelength gives white.

mcqs.stem: A red counter is viewed through a green filter in white light. How does the counter appear?

options.text: Black, because the filter absorbs the red light it reflects
options.rationale: The counter reflects only red; the green filter absorbs red, so no light reaches the eye and the counter looks black.

options.text: Green, because the filter turns the light green as it passes
options.rationale: Assumes objects take on the colour of the filter; a filter can only remove wavelengths already present.

options.text: Red, because the reflected light still gets through it
options.rationale: The light reflected by the counter is red, and a green filter absorbs red, so it does not get through.

options.text: Yellow, because red and green mix inside the filter
options.rationale: Applies colour mixing to a filter; the filter adds no green light of its own for the red to mix with.

mcqs.stem: White light is passed through a red filter and then through a blue filter. What is seen after the second filter?

options.text: White light, because the second filter cancels the first out
options.rationale: Filters act one after the other and only ever subtract; nothing can restore wavelengths that have already been absorbed.

options.text: Almost no light: each filter absorbs what the other passes
options.rationale: The red filter transmits only red and absorbs the rest; the blue filter then absorbs that red, so virtually nothing emerges.

options.text: Purple light, because the red and the blue light add together
options.rationale: Uses the rules for mixing paints or adding light beams, but filters in series remove wavelengths one after another.

options.text: Blue light, since the second filter dyes the light blue
options.rationale: Treats the first filter as colouring the light permanently; the second filter still absorbs the red reaching it.

mcqs.stem: A blue mug is placed in a darkroom lit only by red light. How does the mug appear?

options.text: Purple, since the red light mixes with the mug's own blue
options.rationale: Treats the mug as supplying blue light of its own; in red light there is no blue for it to reflect.

options.text: Blue, since the mug keeps its colour in any lighting
options.rationale: Colour depends on the light falling on the object, not on a fixed property of the object alone.

options.text: Black, as there is no blue light for it to reflect
options.rationale: A blue object reflects blue and absorbs other wavelengths; with only red light present the red is absorbed and no light is reflected.

options.text: Red, since the mug absorbs the red light and shows it
options.rationale: Thinking an object shows the colour it absorbs (m07), a red-absorbing mug is judged red; really absorption gives black.
